FolderMd (https://foldermd.com) might be for you. It's free, and it's fast, and your agents can use it. I made it because I just couldn't handle it anymore.

Yes, you could ask an LLM to choose between 4 options, and sure have it include a confidence score. But at the end of the day it's still LLM-ing and outputting tokens based on the total probability of the chain of tokens that precedes it to figure out what's most likely to come next.

This taps into a lower level of the model, skipping that tedious token generation step, and exposes you to more raw output from the model, e.g. the actual probabilities involved in answering the question.

It still needs to "think like an LLM" to interpret the question, so it's in the same family, but the thought process gets short-circuited once the question is understood and the raw weights are then extracted as pure, weighted probabilities.

Why would you want to use it? What does it enable beyond a traditional LLM?

(a) It's much more efficient (read: cheaper and faster), and not by a %, but an order of magnitude or two. This makes it practical to be used when an LLM isn't, due to its speed and accuracy, which opens up new use cases.

(b) By getting the raw options and weights, you're not getting the LLM's "spin" on the output, nor hallucination risk — instead, you're using an MRI to pull out exactly what it's thinking before the bullshit verbalization engine kicks in.

title: Show HN: Lowlight – Dim your MacBook keyboard backlight below the macOS minimum
text:
I work in a dark room a lot, and even the lowest keyboard backlight setting on my MacBook was too bright. I noticed macOS fades the backlight all the way to zero when it turns off, but the lowest level it lets you pick is noticeably brighter than that.

Lowlight is a small menu bar app that adds extra steps under the macOS minimum, plus the normal range above it. You choose how many extra steps you want. It fades the backlight down and holds it at the step you pick. If you change the keyboard brightness in Control Center, macOS takes back over.

It uses private CoreBrightness APIs, so a future macOS update could break it. It's Apple Silicon only, needs macOS 26, is signed and notarized, and is MIT licensed. You can build it from source with ./build.sh.

I'm happy to answer questions about how it works, or to hear about other Macs it does or doesn't work on.

Why would this be the case? Cloud Run containers and an app runtime like .NET, Java, Go, Rust can inherently be multi-threaded, multi-connection. It can handle up to 1000 concurrent connections per container using just threads and async (assuming sufficient size). Any workload that requires hitting the DB or backend service (S3, etc) is going to I/O bound and sitting in a future most of the time anyways.

The container instances auto-scale by default to a configured n (0 - n) with the option to define specific scale points. If I'm sensitive to high bursts, this can be a matter of scaling at 50% capacity and a warm instance is available while the application still has headway.

Cases where this falls apart: DDoS in which case, I argue that 1) it is better in any case that it falls apart rather than absorbing that type of traffic spike, 2) such traffic is better filtered upstream in any case in an API Gateway + WAF.

I have worked with both types of solutions for different use cases (was invited presenter at Azure Serverless Conf[0]), but my take nowadays is that serverless containers are almost always a better approach since it provides much more flexibility.
